newsitem.title: EGYPT: Cairo economic conference opens with peace calls.
newsitem.headline: Cairo economic conference opens with peace calls.

text.p: A Middle East economic conference opened on Tuesday with a flurry of U.S. and European diplomatic activity aimed at bringing Israel and the PLO closer to an elusive deal on the West Bank town of Hebron.

Outgoing U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher told the forum that agreement on implementing a long-overdue Israeli troop redeployment from Hebron was within reach but his spokesman said it was unlikely to be nailed down in Cairo.

Business took a back seat to diplomacy at the third annual Middle East and North Africa Economic Conference as Christopher met separately with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak.

"The current (Israel-PLO) negotiations have been intensive and at times frustrating. But I believe that a final set of very specific understandings on Hebron is close at hand," Christopher told the conference.

U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Christopher believes, based on his talks with Arafat and Mubarak, that the Hebron negotiations "will succeed -- perhaps not today in Cairo but perhaps in the next week or so."
In his speech, Mubarak said the region would only benefit from economic integration after there is peace.

"Our economies have grown closer...yet this is not close enough, for as long as comprehensive peace on all tracks is not firmly and irreversibly established among us, we will not reap the full benefits of our economic integration," Mubarak said.
Israel and the PLO are currently locked in talks on implementing a partial Israeli pullback from Hebron, where 400 Jewish settlers live among 100,000 Palestinians.
Right-wing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu wants to modify security arrangements set in a Hebron accord signed by the previous Labour-led government. The PLO rejects changing the agreement.
Christopher was due to hold talks with Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy later in the day.
An Israeli government official said no talks had been scheduled at the conference between Israel and the PLO despite the presence of U.S. mediator Dennis Ross.
Once Levy left for home later on Tuesday, the official said, there would be no one in the Israeli delegation authorised to negotiate with Palestinian officials at the conference.

The European Union drew long applause from the mainly Arab businessmen at the conference when it said that land-for-peace, a principle rejected by Netanyahu, must be the basis of a Middle East settlement.
Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring, whose country chairs the EU for the second half of 1996, described the stalemate in peace talks as a crisis of deep concern for Europe.
"The European Union is more than ever convinced that peace in the Middle East depends on the full implementation of the existing agreements between Israel and the Palestinians," he said.
The conference was originally aimed at integrating Israel in the region's economy but the May election of Netanyahu has changed its purpose.

The philosophy now is that Middle East countries must press on with economic reform regardless of political setbacks and that businessmen, rather than just exploiting the opportunities of peace, must add their voices to those of the peacemakers.
The World Economic Forum said the participants, from 92 countries, include 1,500 foreign businesspeople, 500 Egyptian businesspeople and between 1,500 and 2,000 government delegates.

The agenda covers big regional infrastructure projects, classic economic reforms such as privatisation and trade liberalisation, and a heavy dose of networking by the industrialists and investment bankers who are taking part.
